title: Shadiabad Coins and Chanderi Cloth
subtitle: Silver, Thread and the Quiet Engine of Mandu
era: Economy, textiles and coinage of Sultanate Malwa, c. 1405-1562 CE
region: Mandu-Shadiabad, Ujjain, Dhar, Chanderi and Gujarat port routes
moral: Kingdoms stand on the labor of people whose names rarely survive.

sources.citation: Stan Goron and J.P. Goenka, The Coins of the Indian Sultanates (2001), Malwa section
sources.note: Standard catalogue for Malwa tankas, copper issues, mints and bilingual legends.

sources.citation: Abu'l-Fazl, Ain-i-Akbari, Malwa subah revenue and products
sources.note: Mughal-era administrative evidence for Malwa's agriculture, cotton and later opium importance.

sources.citation: Giorgio Riello and Tirthankar Roy, How India Clothed the World (2009); Najaf Haider on currency circulation
sources.note: Modern context for textiles, money and trade routes.

panels.shot: epic bird's-eye over Mandu fort, slowly tightening on a hand spilling silver coins onto fine cotton

dialogue.text: In Mandu’s age of stone palaces, it was not kings but unknown merchants and minters whose silver coins and cotton cloth kept Shadiabad alive.

panels.shot: slow push-in from the dark Narmada valley to sunlit Malwa plateau fields

dialogue.text: On Malwa’s high black-soil plateau, long before the Malwa sultans, farmers coaxed cotton from crackled earth and sent it down dusty tracks to older markets.

panels.shot: medium wide along a caravan road, low-angle tracking beside pack animals

dialogue.text: When Malwa broke from Delhi around 1401, these same tracks began to feed a new hill capital—Shadiabad, the City of Joy—where rulers, priests and soldiers all needed pay and cloth.

panels.shot: interior wide of Mandu bazaar, bustling, slight high angle

dialogue.text: Markets flowered under Mandu’s fortified ridge—coarse cotton for soldiers, finer cloth for court, grain for the kitchens, all meeting under arches of stone and under the eyes of tax-collectors.

panels.shot: close-up of hands weighing and exchanging coins and cloth

dialogue.text: By the fifteenth century, silver tankas of Malwa—square, bright and carefully weighed—moved from weaver to broker to tax official, turning thread into revenue.

panels.shot: moody interior of a mint, diagonal composition with furnaces and anvils

dialogue.text: Behind the bazaar’s noise, the Mandu mint turned bullion into trust—silver melted, cast, and struck with the names of Malwa’s sultans and the hill city Shadiabad.

panels.shot: extreme close-up of a freshly struck coin in tongs

dialogue.text: Some issues bore only Persian and Arabic, others added Nagari—pragmatic marks for a land where clerks, money-changers and villagers read in more than one script.

panels.shot: over-the-shoulder shot of a scribe at a low desk in the mint

dialogue.text: The bilingual coins echoed a bilingual bureaucracy—Ain and ledgers in Persian, local tallies and promises in Nagari—stitched together by habit more than by slogan.

panels.shot: wide shot of Chanderi hillside town, morning mist lifting

dialogue.text: To the northeast lay Chanderi, an old weaving town whose fame for fine cotton predated the Malwa sultans, yet whose looms hummed louder as court orders and traders’ demands grew.

panels.shot: intimate interior of a weaver’s house, low-angle toward loom and spinning

dialogue.text: Weaving stayed a household craft—women spinning, men at looms—yet middlemen linked these rooms to Mandu’s courtyards, and beyond to ports and caravans.

panels.shot: mid-shot of merchant negotiating with weavers, coins and cloth visible

dialogue.speaker: Malwa’s Merchant-Minter
dialogue.text: Finer thread, tighter weave, and I will pay in silver, not copper.

panels.shot: map-like bird's-eye of routes from Malwa to Gujarat and Deccan, overlaid with caravans

dialogue.text: Routes from Ujjain and Chanderi ran to Gujarat’s ports and to the Deccan; Malwa’s cloth and coin travelled with grain, horses and spices toward ships and other sultanates.

panels.shot: dynamic road-level shot of caravan halted at a toll gate with armed guards

dialogue.text: Along those roads, trade meant tax and risk—customs posts, river ferries, rival chiefs and sultanates fighting over the right to squeeze coin from moving bales.

panels.shot: wide shot of battlefield in the distance with smoke, foreground caravan turning aside

dialogue.text: Wars with Gujarat, the Lodis, and later the Mughals were fought partly over these same corridors—control of roads, ferries, markets and their steady stream of silver.

panels.shot: quiet interior of a revenue office, low light, scrolls and coins stacked

dialogue.text: Later, Abu’l-Fazl would list Malwa’s lands, its cotton, and, by then, its opium for the Mughal emperor—proof that these fields and markets kept feeding larger empires.

panels.shot: time-lapse style wide of Mandu palaces fading into Mughal camp, then into ruins

dialogue.text: Mandu fell in 1562 and Malwa’s sultans vanished into chronicles, but their coins kept circulating, their fields stayed planted, and the looms of Chanderi did not fall silent.

panels.shot: extreme close-up of a worn Malwa coin and fragment of Chanderi cloth in palm

dialogue.text: Behind every ruined palace stand unseen hands—farmers of black soil, weavers of fine cotton, and minters of square silver—without whom Malwa’s kings would have ruled over empty stone.
